newsitem.title: UK: British party members want more than doorknocking.
newsitem.headline: British party members want more than doorknocking.

text.p: They push leaflets through doors. They sell tatty second-hand goods in draughty church halls. They respond to appeals for cash at election times. Then they knock on doors to urge voters to support the candidate.
But until quite recently the tens of thousands of Britons who count themselves activists in a major political party exercised little influence when it came to choosing a new party leader.
That was seen as the role of members of parliament. But now the last bastion of legislators' privilege -- the Conservative Party -- looks likely to be stormed.

Its 164 members of parliament decided last week that following precedent they alone would choose the successor to John Major, who is stepping down as leader of the party following its disastrous showing in the May 1 election.

But Sir Archie Hamilton, chairman of the 1922 Committee which decides the rules, pledged to propose a "root and branch reform" of the leadership election process in time for it to be considered at the party's annual conference in October.

Even this compromise brought howls of protest from members who pointed out that Scotland and Wales would play no part in choosing Major's successor in a process beginning on June 10 -- the party lost all its seats in both of them on May 1.

"It is a huge disappointment. It shows an arrogance on the part of the parliamentary party, of the kind which lost us the last election," said John Strafford, a member of the party's National Executive.

"Over the coming months, they (activists) will insist on a complete reorganisation of the party structure which will take power away from Central Office (headquarters) and the MPs," commentator Peter Oborne wrote in Sunday's Express newspaper.
The question now is whether the Conservatives can agree a new leadership election system without the rancour and schism which surrounded the process when Labour went through it.

In January 1981 a Labour Party conference decided future leaders should be chosen by an electoral college in which the party's trade union paymasters had 40 percent of the votes, MPs 30 percent and rank-and-file constituency members 30 percent.
The day after the conference, four moderate former Labour cabinet ministers met in Limehouse, London angry that the largely left-wing unions had been given such influence.

Their Limehouse Declaration called for a realignment of British politics and their later defection with more than a dozen other Labour MPs to the Social Democratic Party condemned Labour to opposition until just three weeks ago.

Labour has now changed its leadership election format. The unions are on an equal footing with the MPs and the constituency members in the electoral college and any candidate must be nominated by an eighth of the parliamentary party.
The minority Liberal Democrats, heirs to merger between the SDP and the old Liberal Party, are more democratic still.
While a candidate for the leadership must be nominated by at least a fifth of his or her parliamentary colleagues, the election is then on a simple one party member one vote basis.
Labour has been gaining members in recent years and the Liberal Democrat membership is steady.

Some observers link the haemorrhage of members from the Conservative party -- the failure to attract new blood has pushed the average age of a card-carrying Conservative up to 64 -- to its lack of grass roots democracy.
